title: Paul Asked Christians a Shocking Question: “Should I Take Christ’s Members and Join Them to a Prostitute?”
paragraphs: Paul Asked Christians a Shocking Question: “Should I Take Christ’s Members and Join Them to a Prostitute?”
Paul was not merely warning Christians about sexual sin. He was confronting them with a terrifyingly intimate truth: what you do with your body involves Someone else now—because you belong to Christ.
There are Bible verses we read quietly.
And then there are Bible verses that seem to grab us by the shoulders.
This is one of them.
“Shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an harlot?”
That is essentially the question Paul fires at the Corinthian believers in 1 Corinthians 6:15.
It is deliberately shocking.
Almost uncomfortable.
Maybe that was the point.
Because Corinth knew how to make sin look normal.
And if we are painfully honest, so do we.
Different century.
Different streets.
Different technology.
Same human heart.
Today the prostitute may not be standing where everyone can see her.
She may be behind a locked screen.
The affair may begin with a message nobody else knows exists.
Pornography can enter a bedroom without opening the front door.
Lust can hide beneath an innocent-looking search history.
Emotional infidelity can disguise itself as friendship.
Sexual compromise can be renamed “freedom.”
And a Christian can learn how to worship publicly while secretly feeding something that is slowly hollowing out the soul.
Then Paul asks a question so severe that it destroys every comfortable excuse:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
The Greek is even worth seeing:
Οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν μέλη Χριστοῦ ἐστιν;
Ouk oidate hoti ta sōmata hymōn melē Christou estin?
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
Then comes the blow:
ἄρας οὖν τὰ μέλη τοῦ Χριστοῦ ποιήσω πόρνης μέλη; μὴ γένοιτο.
Aras oun ta melē tou Christou poiēsō pornēs melē? Mē genoito.
“Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? May it never be!”
That final expression matters.
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
Paul uses this forceful Greek expression elsewhere when rejecting an idea with horror. Depending on context, it carries the force of “May it never be,” “Absolutely not,” or “God forbid.”
Paul is not treating sexual immorality like an embarrassing little mistake respectable Christians should avoid discussing.
He takes it directly to our union with Jesus Christ.
Your body matters because Christ redeemed the whole person.
Your Christianity does not stop at your neck.
Jesus is not Lord only of your theology.
He is Lord of your eyes.
Your hands.
Your imagination.
Your sexuality.
Your private messages.
Your browser history.
Your bedroom.
Your loneliness.
Your desires.
Your body.
Everything.
And perhaps that is why this passage hurts.
Because some people reading this love Jesus...
and still have secrets.
Maybe you promised God it was the last time.
Then you went back.
Maybe you deleted everything.
Then downloaded it again.
Maybe nobody knows about the messages.
Maybe your spouse sleeps beside you without knowing where your imagination has been.
Maybe you have never physically touched another person, but lust has constructed an entire hidden universe inside you.
Maybe you are carrying memories of things you did years ago and wondering whether God still sees you as contaminated.
Maybe sexual sin was done to you, and whenever passages like this are preached carelessly, you somehow walk away carrying shame for another person's evil.
Hear this clearly:
Being sinned against is not the same as willingly committing the sin Paul condemns.
The abused person does not carry the moral guilt of the abuser.
Jesus does not look at the wounded and confuse the wound with rebellion.
But when we willingly embrace sexual immorality, Scripture refuses to let us pretend that our bodies are spiritually irrelevant.
Paul continues:
“Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, ‘The two will become one flesh.’”
Then Paul gives us the contrast that changes everything:
“But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.”
Read that again.
Joined to the Lord.
Christianity is not merely believing certain statements about Jesus.
It is belonging to Jesus.

Paul's argument reaches back to the “one flesh” language of Genesis 2:24. Sexual union is therefore not treated in Scripture as meaningless physical recreation. It carries a bodily significance rooted in God's design for marriage.
That is why Paul's command is not casual:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not keep it bookmarked.
Not see how close you can get without technically crossing your personal line.
Not call temptation harmless because nobody has discovered it yet.
Flee.
Joseph understood something like this centuries earlier when Potiphar's wife tried to pull him into sexual sin.
He did not stay to demonstrate how spiritually mature he was.
He ran.
Sometimes the holiest thing your feet can do is leave.
Sometimes repentance looks like blocking a number.
Deleting an account.
Ending a secret relationship.
Installing accountability.
Confessing to a mature believer.
Getting out of the room.
Turning off the device.
Stopping the conversation.
Bringing what thrives in darkness into the light.
But there is another side of this passage that must never be forgotten.
Paul was writing to Christians in Corinth.
And Corinth was not populated by people with spotless histories.
Only a few verses earlier, Paul gives a devastating list of sins and then writes one of the most beautiful sentences ever addressed to morally ruined people:
“And such were some of you.”
Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε.
Kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That word is thunder.
Your history may explain part of your story.
It does not have authority to write your ending.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not grace that pretends sin does not matter.
Grace that proves sin does not get the final word.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing at a distance from filthy people waiting for them to clean themselves.

The Gospel is the holy Son of God entering our ruined world, bearing sin at the cross, dying for sinners, rising victorious from the grave, and calling guilty people to repent, believe, and belong to Him.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by redeeming people who could never redeem themselves.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not permission to continue in bondage.
Grace opens the prison door.
Paul's message eventually reaches this breathtaking conclusion:
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?”
Then:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price.”
And therefore:
“Glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
The Christian body is not worthless.
Not disposable.
Not merely biological machinery carrying around the “spiritual” part of you.
You were bought with a price.
And the price was infinitely greater than silver.
Greater than gold.
Greater than anything you could ever repay.
Peter describes believers as redeemed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with “the precious blood of Christ.”
So when temptation whispers,
“Nobody will know...”
remember:
Christ knows whose body this is.
When lust whispers,
“You need this...”
remember:
Christ is better.
When shame whispers,
“You are disgusting and God could never want you again...”
remember:
“And such were some of you.”
When your past whispers,
“You will always be what you did...”
remember:
“You were washed.”
When condemnation whispers,
“You crossed the line too many times...”
run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
Repentance is not running away from the Savior because you are dirty.
Repentance is turning from sin and running to the Savior because only He can make sinners clean.
Maybe that is why you are reading this right now.
Maybe beneath all the Christian language, inspirational posts, church attendance, worship music, and “I'm doing okay” answers...
you are exhausted from hiding.
You love Jesus.
But something has been eating you alive in secret.
Then stop protecting what Christ is calling you to surrender.
Bring it into the light.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more relapse.
Not when you finally feel worthy enough to pray.
Now.
Tell Jesus the truth He already knows.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help where needed.
Cut off access to what keeps dragging you backward.
And when you fall, do not reinterpret grace as permission to remain on the ground.
Get up and return to Christ.
Again.
Because Christian freedom is not the freedom to give your body to every appetite that demands it.
Christian freedom is finally being free to belong completely to the One who purchased you.
And perhaps somebody you know is fighting this battle silently.
They will never announce it.
They may never post about it.
They may sit beside you in church.
They may preach.
Lead worship.
Raise children.
Smile in photographs.
Then go home and lose another private war.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It does not.
Christ alone saves, entirely by grace, received through faith.
Send it privately to the friend who has been disappearing spiritually.
You are not your own. You were bought with a price.
You do not need to publish intimate details. Wisdom and appropriate privacy still matter.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall somebody has spent years building.
And if God has used Gospel Warrior to strengthen your walk with Christ, you can help us keep placing Christ-centered biblical truth in front of people who desperately need it.
They are not substitutes for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, or personal discipleship. They are simply opportunities to participate in spreading Gospel-centered resources.
Then invite somebody else to come with you.
A family member.
A struggling Christian.
Someone who has grown lukewarm.
Someone ashamed of their past.
Someone who does not believe yet.
Someone who desperately needs to discover that Jesus Christ is not frightened by sinners who finally stop hiding.
Because Paul's shocking question was never written merely to make sexually broken people feel dirty.
It was written to remind Christians who they belong to.
You are Christ's.
Your body matters.
Holiness matters.
Repentance matters.
What happens in secret matters.
But grace matters too.
The cross matters.
The empty tomb matters.
And Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Your scandal may be real.
Your consequences may be real.
Your wounds may be real.
Your battle may be real.
But none of them are greater than the Savior who died and rose again.
So flee what is destroying you.
Run toward Christ.
Come out of hiding.
You were bought with a price.
Glorify God with the life He redeemed.
And never forget this:
The sin you thought would become the final sentence of your story may become the very place where the grace of Jesus writes, “Redeemed.”
